Q26.text: The academic system encourages absolute sacrifice for the sake of success, which is neither healthy nor fair. The lack of opportunities creates a cutthroat-type of environment, where too often the ones climbing to the top do so at the expense of others, or by forging data to publish in high-impact journals. At the same time, those with families, or other responsibilities - generally women, let's be real -, or those who need to sustain a job to pay for the PhD, cannot afford to sacrifice their entire time to research, and are easily pushed to the sidelines. The latter also speaks to the difficulty for PhDs to compete in a global job market, as the financial burden is widely different around the world. Likewise, PhD programmes vary immensely in quality - a 3-year PhD graduate whose project was spoon-fed to them by their supervisor will not have developed the same skills as a 5-year PhD who had to design their own research project, but they will compete in an almost equal footing for a position.

But regardless I turned out to be a shit scientist -- no publications (inc. in sight), no conferences attended even with a poster, I am not sure whether my research will yield something presentable. I cannot network or promote myself. I do not write well. If I graduate without a paper, I am looking at a mediocre lab postdoc position at best with median year salary ~$45k. I do not know how I will afford rent, savings for the future, taking care of my parents -- I am the only child. I do not know whether I can land an industry job in the competitive environment over-producing PhDs.  I heard about people who get scholarships and earn 30-50% above the typical postdoc salary. They apply for grants and quickly become PIs to earn their lower three figures. Or they aim for green cards through H1B or EB2, paying for the mistake of being born in a shit third-world country, through living off $45k for several years to then end a better paying job in industry. Both options require publishing at least three first author papers, having citations, getting funding, networking -- all the things I don't see myself doing as of now. There are labs that are more collaborative and people end up helping with other peoples' projects and with more papers in the end. I am not in one of them. People who chose different majors -- programming or medicine -- can get bioinformatician or clinical fellow salaries doing same science next to me but earning two times more. Their salaries approaching market because they have a choice. I do not have a choice. Why did no one stop me at any point? How did I end up here? What am I going to do in the future? I think academic system feeds on people like me luring us with promises of meaningful job and hard work paying off and shits us out. It is not healthy to work weekends. It is not healthy to sometimes go months without seeing any progress. It is not healthy to over-sell results in publications just to survive in this environment.

Q26.text: Sadly, the only important criteria for success in academia is the amount of published material. This often leads to rivals among senior and junior researchers, where the former is more likely to get the credit even for work performed by the junior person (e.g. author list on publications). A race for publishing is so intense since most staff contracts (PhD stipends) depend on the amount and impact of publications within a certain time frame (e.g. 3 years for a PhD in life sciences).      Unfortunately, moral standards at some German institutions are at its lowest level: A new research institute that is yet to receive its academic recognition will rather ignore repeated complaints on staff injustice and academic misconduct than risk a bad reputation. Likewise, a young PI will refuse to protect and stand behind a victim of sabotage and pretend all is fine, as long as there is a possibility for a new publication from the person doing the injustice.       PhD students are often subjected to exploitation with no protection since at the end of the day everyone needs that critical reference letter to pursue the next step in an academic career.

Q55.text: There are far more opportunities available for postgraduate students in the USA/EU, many of my friends and colleagues in the field who did their Masters degree abroad easily found PhD positions at top ranking institutions despite having no publications in the field (or often any publications at all) and mediocre grades. Many reviewers force us to cite their own papers in the manuscript before accepting our publication (despite being anonymous it is obvious when the authorship fields of these papers all contain the same researcher). Often the work is not significant or the results are less competative than other papers already cited in the manuscript.  In short it is very difficult (but certainly possible) to get in to the right networks for your career if you're coming from the wrong institution. Q60.text: Thanks for performing this survey. This is an extremely important topic that is often overlooked. We are looked at as cheap labor (and often young) labor that needs to pay their dues. But often it comes at the cost of our mental and physical health. My mental and physical health has significantly declined over the past 4 years that I've been in my PhD program. I've definitely experienced depression and anxiety, and have had many more visits to the doctor for physical health problems. A back problem from sitting for 12 hours a day at the computer, problems with my hands from typing so much, other problems from increasing my drinking (to cope with stress), a urinary tract infection from holding my urine too long because I don't have time to pee because I am working; I've often put off medical appointments due to lack of time as well. Students often put off their health like they are in survival mode and tell themselves "it's okay to not be healthy for a while" because when you are done with the program you will have time to be healthy. But after years of putting off your health and happiness, living in "survival mode" becomes unbearable. That combined with feeling like you have no control over your own labor nor are getting compensated a livable wage for it can be extremely depressing. Granted some students are predisposed to having more health problems than others as a result of the stressors of a PhD program--however, there are major problems with the system and culture of PhD education that need to be fixed to support student health.

Q26.text: O sistema acadêmico da república tcheca é bastante focado em produção.  Não se importa muito a defesa de uma tese, da ideia em si.  Apenas vejo que o programas de PhD em geral esqueceram da onde vem a sigla Ph.D e não discutem mais as coisas no âmbito argumentativo.  Não importam tanto com o racional do projeto, com a hipótese do projeto... e a defesa argumentativa que deveria ser feita.  Maioria dos projetos vejo que começa simplesmente por que temos dinheiro e estrutura. Mas não porque temos um grande racional e uma justificativa para tentar lançar uma hipótese a ser defendida por provas a posteriori.    Na minha concepção,  Tudo deveria iniciar com uma ideia sólida.  Uma hipótese a qual todos não consigam derrubar com argumentos. Sendo interessante alocar recursos escassos para responder uma pergunta da qual necessita-se de uma resposta a posteriori.    O sistema então acaba valorizando bastante dados soltos, contudo ainda sim são resultados. E acaba desvalorizando o tempo 'perdido' no campo das ideias.   A quantidade muitas vezes parece ser mais importante do que a qualidade . Infelizmente vejo que o sistema recompensa este tipo de mentalidade.  No Brasil (país onde fiz meu mestrado), não era diferente.   Com isso , o sistema que criamos é um sistema preocupado com técnicos. Pessoas que vangloriam por saber determinada técnica.  Pois em teoria, isto traz mais produção.  As pessoas não entendem que aprender técnica é apenas uma questão de tempo e prática. Não precisa de raciocínio lógico. Sendo que em muitos institutos grandes, você de fato tem técnicos e facilities para fazer o trabalho técnico para você.   No entanto, técnica pode ser aplicada mil vezes... mas se não estiver denfendendo uma ideia não fará nenhum sentido fazer por fazer.   Acredito que precisamos fazer um esforço para mudar esta mentalidade nos institutos ao redor do mundo.  A revista Nature é muito conceituada e acredito que ela representa bem a amostragem dos institutos que de fato estão preocupados em mover o mundo através de ideias.    Pedro Zeni

Q60.text: I think a lot of the uncertainty about phD careers arises from the vastly different experience each trainee has during graduate school. For example, one trainee may work 70 hours per week, manage a budget, run multiple projects at once, and publish 4 first-author publications as well as a handful of non-first author publications. Meanwhile, another trainee in the same department might work 30 hours per week on their own personal project, is well-read, becomes a member in multiple peer groups/societies, maintains a vibrant social life and extracurricular agenda, and overall is a more well-rounded person. While the first person is likely to move on to a competitive academic post-doc, which of these two is most competitive for the non-academic position? Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system works on networking and knowing people, including the publication system. The fact that the student has to obtain a recommendation from the supervisor for any post-doctoral position is an example feature of a system that is stuck in the old era. And the student is extremely lucky if the supervisor is friendly, knowledgeable and most importantly, has the welfare of the student and their career as one of his/her priorities. I was unlucky. But, in my opinion, it is the fault of the system to have such a highly skewed power structure. The student is guaranteed to be exploited, by design.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system encourages absolute sacrifice for the sake of success, which is neither healthy nor fair. The lack of opportunities creates a cutthroat-type of environment, where too often the ones climbing to the top do so at the expense of others, or by forging data to publish in high-impact journals. At the same time, those with families, or other responsibilities - generally women, let's be real -, or those who need to sustain a job to pay for the PhD, cannot afford to sacrifice their entire time to research, and are easily pushed to the sidelines. The latter also speaks to the difficulty for PhDs to compete in a global job market, as the financial burden is widely different around the world. Likewise, PhD programmes vary immensely in quality - a 3-year PhD graduate whose project was spoon-fed to them by their supervisor will not have developed the same skills as a 5-year PhD who had to design their own research project, but they will compete in an almost equal footing for a position.

Q55.text: Create a plan early, and refine it as often as necessary. A flawed or incomplete plan is better than no plan at all. Q26.text: A well-veiled pyramid scheme, honestly -- the people at the top extract labour from those below under the guise of mentorship and training, and the grant system actively incentivises PIs to treat graduate students as inexpensive instruments rather than scholars in development. Q16.text: The leave situation has been significant -- I requested personal leave for a family emergency and was told, not unkindly but very clearly, that my timeline couldn't accommodate it. And I've heard my PI make comments about maternity leave that I found genuinely alarming, the kind that signal how students with caregiving needs are likely to be treated. it's not illegal, probably, but it shapes the culture in ways that are hard to document and easy to dismiss.

Q55.text: How to vet a PI -- not for research fit, which I obsessed over, but for actual mentorship culture: how they talk about former students, whether they've ever protected a student at personal cost, how they respond to the word "no." I asked none of those questions and I paid for it.

Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: My PhD program advertised 4 weeks of time off per year, and a generous maternal leave policy.  The promise of a work-life balance lured me it, but my PI does not allow this much time off, and I often end up working through the weekend. This results in even lower total work output, because I'm tired and depressed all the time and more likely to make mistakes.  My PI has also remarked to at least one student that not electing to come back from maternity leave early means you don't care enough about science to be successful.

Q26.text: Experience in academia depends greatly on the department, environment, and university one is attending. Q26.text:
Extractive. That's the word I keep coming back to. You give your best years, your health, your relationships, your geographic freedom — and in return you get stipend that barely covers rent, a CV with no publications, and supervisor who's too busy to actually mentor you. The whole thing is designed to produce cheap labor for PIs, not scientists.

And if you're international, you're doubly trapped. Visa status means you cant just quit, cant just pivot. You grind through experiments that don't work while watching people back home build actual careers and actual lives. And when something happens — a death, a crisis — you don't even get to go home.

It's not that I failed the system, honestly. the system was never designed for people like me to succeed.

Q16.text:
The mental health support is a joke. one counselling session every six weeks if you're lucky, with someone who has no idea what a PhD actually involves. And you're supposed to just keep pipetting, keep smiling at lab meetings, keep pretending the stipend is enough when reagents cost more than you make in a month.

Also the complete lack of acknowledgment that wet-lab PhDs are physically exhausting. It's not just intellectual stress — it's standing for hours, chemical exposure, failed experiments that you cant explain and have to repeat anyway. Nobody talks about the physical toll.

And honestly, the loneliness. Not just missing family. The specific loneliness of being surrounded by people and still having no one who actually sees what you're going through.

Q55.text:
That publications are currency and nothing else matters. Not your work ethic, not your hours, not how good your questions are. If you don't publish, you don't exist in this field. I spent years being told "the work speaks for itself" — it doesn't. The work means nothing without a paper attached.

And honestly, that visa dependency would make every bad situation ten times worse. I had no exit. That's not a minor inconvenience, it's a trap.

Q41.text: Anything that gets me out of academia. Industry, government, I don't care anymore.

Q60.text:
Just that I hope someone actually reads these and doesn't just aggregate them into a statistic. There are real people behind these answers who are genuinely struggling, not just "experiencing stress" in some clinical sense.

The system keeps producing surveys like this and very little changes. So I'm skeptical. But I filled it in anyway because maybe one day it adds up to something.

Q17.text: The autonomy, I guess. No one tells me when to show up. That's about it rn.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I studied for over 8 years to be where I am now. I do not have student debt. I was a straight As student in school and in college. But regardless I turned out to be a shit scientist -- no publications (inc. in sight), no conferences attended even with a poster, I am not sure whether my research will yield something presentable. I cannot network or promote myself. I do not write well. If I graduate without a paper, I am looking at a mediocre lab postdoc position at best with median year salary ~$45k. I do not know how I will afford rent, savings for the future, taking care of my parents -- I am the only child. I do not know whether I can land an industry job in the competitive environment over-producing PhDs.  I heard about people who get scholarships and earn 30-50% above the typical postdoc salary. They apply for grants and quickly become PIs to earn their lower three figures. Or they aim for green cards through H1B or EB2, paying for the mistake of being born in a shit third-world country, through living off $45k for several years to then end a better paying job in industry. Both options require publishing at least three first author papers, having citations, getting funding, networking -- all the things I don't see myself doing as of now. There are labs that are more collaborative and people end up helping with other peoples' projects and with more papers in the end. I am not in one of them. People who chose different majors -- programming or medicine -- can get bioinformatician or clinical fellow salaries doing same science next to me but earning two times more. Their salaries approaching market because they have a choice. I do not have a choice. Why did no one stop me at any point? How did I end up here? What am I going to do in the future? I think academic system feeds on people like me luring us with promises of meaningful job and hard work paying off and shits us out. It is not healthy to work weekends. It is not healthy to sometimes go months without seeing any progress. It is not healthy to over-sell results in publications just to survive in this environment.

Two of my close relatives died and I did not come to say my good byes. My boyfriend is doing PhD in a different country. I hate this.

Q16.text: The job market is honestly what worries me most, outside of funding. Q55.text: How much the publication timeline depends on your supervisor. I would have chosen PI more carefully, and asked much more direct questions before agreeing to join a lab.

Q17.text: Intellectual freedom, mostly. I get to pursue questions that genuinely interest me, which isn't something many jobs offer. It's hard to separate that from the frustrations -- the funding stress, the waiting on publications -- but the research itself is still what keeps me going.

Q26.text: I fortunately got salary and budget for my own research.  However, I have to pay for tax, national health insurance, pension insurance, and tuition fee from my salary.  Furthermore, only 20-30% of PhD candidates can  recieve such money. I now get salary from Japan society for the promotion of science (JSPS), a national organization without employment contract. Thus I will not get unemployment insurance even if I cannot get postdoc job after my getting PhD. I don't think Japanese government seriously concern the future of scientific research in Japan.

Q60.text: I think the relationship between industry and academia is perverse. Industry profits from public investment in academic research, and has no obligations to provide any societal benefit with those profits. National or non-profit labs should take academic research to the public. Public investment, public profits, societal benefits. The pharmaceutical industry is an exemplar of this relationship. Every drug has relied on public funding, yet no publicly funded patent returns those investments back into scientific grants. This change occurred during Reagan administration when patents became university rather than government grant office property.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Sadly, the only important criteria for success in academia is the amount of published material. This often leads to rivals among senior and junior researchers, where the former is more likely to get the credit even for work performed by the junior person (e.g. author list on publications). A race for publishing is so intense since most staff contracts (PhD stipends) depend on the amount and impact of publications within a certain time frame (e.g. 3 years for a PhD in life sciences).      Unfortunately, moral standards at some German institutions are at its lowest level: A new research institute that is yet to receive its academic recognition will rather ignore repeated complaints on staff injustice and academic misconduct than risk a bad reputation. Likewise, a young PI will refuse to protect and stand behind a victim of sabotage and pretend all is fine, as long as there is a possibility for a new publication from the person doing the injustice.       PhD students are often subjected to exploitation with no protection since at the end of the day everyone needs that critical reference letter to pursue the next step in an academic career.

Q26.text: The academic system feels like it was designed for people without real financial obligations — where a stipend is supplemental income, not a lifeline. For those of us carrying debt and family responsibilities, the math never quite works out, and the institution mostly doesnt notice or adjust. Supervision accountability is essentially absent, and structural support is whatever you can piece together on your own. Honestly its been pretty disillusioning, and I say that as someone who came in genuinely wanting to do good research.

Q16.text: The mental health side of things, honestly. There's a kind of ambient stress that accumulates when you're not sure if your funding holds, your supervisor isnt particularly invested, and you're watching peers leave for industry jobs that pay three times what you're making. I dont think I fully anticipated how isolating it would feel, and the university's wellness resources are more of a checkbox than an actual support system.

Q55.text: That the stipend math doesn't work if you have actual debt. I came in thinking I could manage it, and I was wrong, and no one in the department thought to mention that or help me think it through.

Q16.text: Peer review needs to be more rigorous; initial screening for falsified data, re-used images, etc. The quality of our peer review determines the quality of our science and collective understanding. We need a generation that is more discerning and doesn't just trust something because it is published; in that sense, I'm worried about the state and fate of science.

Q26.text: Broken, and not in a fixable-with-minor-tweaks way. The incentive structures are misaligned at EVERY level -- PIs are rewarded for grants and publications, not for actually developing the people in their labs. Students are cheap labor dressed up as apprentices. And the financial model is genuinely unsustainable if you're trying to do anything resembling a normal adult life afterward -- buying a house, starting a family, paying off debt. There are real structural fixes on the table, shorter programs, meaningful PI accountability, stipends tied to actual cost of living. But the people with power to change it benefit from keeping it exactly as it is, honestly. That's what makes it so hard to stay optimistic about reform.

Q16.text: The mental health piece, tbh. It gets talked about in the abstract but never treated as the structural outcome it actually is -- like, of course people are struggling when you underpay them, isolate them in a lab with a checked-out PI, and dangle an increasingly mythological career at the end. Late-stage is genuinely rough in ways I didn't anticipate. And there's no one institutionally positioned to notice or care, so you just... build a support system outside the lab and hope it holds.

Q55.text: That the PI relationship is essentially the whole thing. Everything else -- the department, the program prestige, the funding -- is secondary noise. A checked-out supervisor can hollow out five years of your life in ways that are really hard to recover from, and there's basically no institutional recourse when it happens. I would have asked completely different questions during lab rotations if I'd understood that early enough.

Q41.text: Management consulting, executive recruiting, or policy. Anything that uses analytical skills without the academic dysfunction.

Q60.text: Not really. I hope someone with actual institutional power reads this and does something with it, but I'm not holding my breath.

Q17.text: The intellectual environment, honestly. Being surrounded by people who genuinely care about ideas -- that part is real, and I'll miss it. It's just not enough to compensate for everything else the system puts you through.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Broken. The wages are skewed. The incentives for faculty to publish in high impact factor journals make graduate students not have as many publications. There's fierce competition for grants which incentivizes cheating. The goal for the graduate student is to graduate and find employment but the goal for the faculty is to produce research and papers, thus these are at conflict. As a grad student becomes well trained, the faculty don't want to let them graduate because they have cheap, well trained, labor. Academic postdoc positions are the same. They're lowly paid but highly competent individuals. Faculty in universities still aren't aware of the data regarding competition for new faculty positions (despite serving on search panels). The whole system is broken.

Q16.text: The biggest, most overwhelming concern for the entirety of my PhD is trying to find good employment afterwards that can cover my student debt and allow me to start a family. Unfortunately, academic postdoc positions in the US do not pay enough to do this, which means I have to find a non-default path.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: Good science and good management/leadership do not overlap. My PI is a great scientist but he is a TERRIBLE manager. This is likely why the average time to degree for my lab is 8 years when the department average is 6.5. He's incredibly hands off, provides no positive feedback, and discourages many things. You have to fight tooth and nail to get what you want unless you're his favorite student.

Q41.label: What type of career are you interested in pursuing after your graduate degree?
Q41.text: One that intersects with the life sciences but doesn't require bench research. I'd be happy continuing computational (genomic) research. I enjoy meetings and administrative/leadership/management work. Perhaps a policy analyst and strategy position. I'm currently targeting management consulting, executive recruiting, and policy analyst positions for application.

Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: We don't have an excess of people with PhD degrees. The world needs more highly educated people. We have a broken system that provides incentive for poor quality of life for graduate students and postdocs -- low pay, aggressive competition, long hours, discouragement from leaving the academic environment. This can be fixed, but it needs to be a top-down move away from the publish or perish environment. Even more faculty positions aren't necessary. Staff research positions would be great. Tenure-track teaching positions (divide the labor so some faculty are almost full time research, many are teaching) would make a significant difference. Put hard caps on graduate programs (6 years) to force program progression. Many people in my program don't defend their prospectus until year 5 which is COMPLETELY inappropriate. There is no department or university recourse for this.

Q26.text: A self-reinforcing hierarchy that rewards compliance and punishes accountability. PIs face essentially no consequences for exploiting students, and institutional incentives -- grants, publications, rankings -- make this structural, not incidental.

Q16.text: The mental health dimension — chronic anxiety, isolation, the particular corrosiveness of having your competence questioned by someone who benefits from your uncertainty. It doesn't show up in exit surveys because people leave too depleted to describe it accurately.

Q55.text: That supervisor selection is effectively irreversible once you're in, and that the vetting process is almost entirely one-sided. You interview them in theory; in practice you're auditioned. Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: There are far more opportunities available for postgraduate students in the USA/EU, many of my friends and colleagues in the field who did their Masters degree abroad easily found PhD positions at top ranking institutions despite having no publications in the field (or often any publications at all) and mediocre grades. As a department we also regularly experience what we perceive as discrimination from reviewers towards third world universities, even when the results are objectively valuable and can be quickly reproduced with no effort (such as running a script with fully free and open source code). Many reviewers force us to cite their own papers in the manuscript before accepting our publication (despite being anonymous it is obvious when the authorship fields of these papers all contain the same researcher). Often the work is not significant or the results are less competative than other papers already cited in the manuscript.  In short it is very difficult (but certainly possible) to get in to the right networks for your career if you're coming from the wrong institution. The quality of your research is largely irrelevant, even in fields where problems have objective and established metrics for the quality of solutions.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The lack of respect for my job as a PhD student from the academy, some of my peers and society in general. My PhD is a job, I work full time on it and however I am only payed 50% (in Germany) of my salary because I am "student". When I complain that this is unfair, that I am not being payed for my full work hours or my extra hours (that are always expected of me as a PhD student); I am told that 1) I should be grateful for even getting paid, other disciplines are not 2) I benefit from student discounts so I should not complain for receiving less (I would happily give away my student discounts if I was payed a full salary!) 3) I should be happy because I am doing my passion job (passion is not going to feed me in my retirement). Not being entitle to a full salary, extra hours or even a contract that will allow us to receive some help after our working years is destroying our future before it even starts.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: I did not start my PhD directly after the masters, I was working sometime as a research assistant. So by the time I decided to do a PhD I knew exactly why I was doing it and what were some of the possible challenges. As such I was prepared to keep going despite having to change my first PI (due to PI sickness) and restarting my PhD after 2 years and despite having a new PI now that is not meeting my expectations. So, I do think i was prepared to do a PhD when I started. Personally, from what I see around me, I would just tell everyone to not do a PhD right after the master/bachelor but to take their time and to find if a PhD is really what they want to do.

Q26.text: The system has genuine intellectual appeal, and when things work as they should the research culture is genuinely stimulating -- but structurally, the funding shortfalls, opaque decision-making, and faculty politics create conditions that are honestly pretty obstructive, and coming in with 25 years of professional experience I thought I understood institutional dysfunction, but academia operates on its own particular logic that seems more focused on protecting incumbent interests than actually supporting the research it claims to exist for.

Q16.text: The lab access situation has been a persistent concern honestly -- being blocked from my preferred lab because of overcrowding and what I can only call administrative paralysis left me in limbo for longer than it should have, and while I've adapted by spanning multiple labs, that arrangement carries its own coordination costs that nobody seems to account for in any official capacity.

Q55.text: The informal power structures -- who actually controls lab space, who has the ear of the graduate coordinator, which alliances determine resource allocation -- operate completely independently of the formal rules you're given at orientation, and honestly if I'd understood that the map bears almost no relationship to the territory in terms of how decisions actually get made, I would have invested far more energy early on in cultivating those informal relationships rather than assuming the processes would work as advertised.

Q41.text: Neuroscience research, integrating my clinical and multidisciplinary background -- ideally applied rather than purely academic, given what I've seen of how universities actually function.

Q60.text: It's been a useful exercise to articulate these experiences, and I hope the data contributes to something meaningful -- the structural issues I've described aren't unique to my situation, I suspect, and if this research helps surface systemic patterns around funding, lab access, and institutional transparency then it's worth the time. The one thing I'd add is that mature-age students with professional backgrounds face a particular kind of dislocation that the university doesn't seem to have frameworks for -- we're not the typical 24-year-old and the support structures reflect that assumption pretty comprehensively.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly -- being able to pursue questions that actually matter to me after 25 years of working within other people's agendas is genuinely satisfying, even if the institutional context makes it harder than it should be.

Q26.text: Lack of funding and PhD students converting from full time to part time officially but actually working full time so they can get through the experimental workload has crowded out my preferred lab choice & I could not get a position due to lack of funding and overcrowding. I am now trying to do the same research under neuroscience and link into different labs as I design an experiment. The benefit is I am not tied to any one lab but it increases the stress around the experimental stages of my degree due to not gaining access to a lab or failing to get funding. I was very disappointed by the faculty allowing students to be enrolled part time but work full time as this also was not reflected in lab availability as well as very costly in lab equipment and consumables being used at a full time rate rather than a part time rate which drained the lab budget causing the lab to almost run out of money and engage in talks of letting go of the post docs because of funding issues around ability to pay them.

Q26.text: I have a very dismal view of the academic system in general. The majority of my work has almost nothing to do with "education" and instead is truly work being done for my professor that has very little chance of benefiting me or advancing my career independently. Q26.text: Fundamentally extractive. Attitude from faculty/PIs that graduate students exist to generate outputs, putting off any real mentorship until it's too late, normalizing hours that would be illegal in any other professional context -- it all adds up. Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: Thanks for performing this survey. This is an extremely important topic that is often overlooked. We are looked at as cheap labor (and often young) labor that needs to pay their dues. But often it comes at the cost of our mental and physical health. My mental and physical health has significantly declined over the past 4 years that I've been in my PhD program. I've definitely experienced depression and anxiety, and have had many more visits to the doctor for physical health problems. A back problem from sitting for 12 hours a day at the computer, problems with my hands from typing so much, other problems from increasing my drinking (to cope with stress), a urinary tract infection from holding my urine too long because I don't have time to pee because I am working; I've often put off medical appointments due to lack of time as well. Students often put off their health like they are in survival mode and tell themselves "it's okay to not be healthy for a while" because when you are done with the program you will have time to be healthy. But after years of putting off your health and happiness, living in "survival mode" becomes unbearable. That combined with feeling like you have no control over your own labor nor are getting compensated a livable wage for it can be extremely depressing. Granted some students are predisposed to having more health problems than others as a result of the stressors of a PhD program--however, there are major problems with the system and culture of PhD education that need to be fixed to support student health.

Q26.text: Honestly, it rewards output over people -- publications, grants, metrics -- and there's kind of an unspoken assumption that if you're struggling, that's your problem to sort out. Q16.text: The job market, honestly -- I keep hearing that academic positions are increasingly rare, and I'm not entirely sure where chemistry PhDs actually end up outside academia or pharma. I haven't fully figured out what I want yet, so the uncertainty is kind of unsettling, even if I'm trying to stay open about it.

Q55.text: That the career path is a lot less linear than anyone tells you going in. I kind of assumed there was a clear track -- finish, publish, postdoc, job -- but that script doesn't hold for most people, and knowing that earlier might have made me a bit less anxious about not having plan yet.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly — being able to dig into a problem that actually matters and follow it wherever it goes. I also enjoy the people I work with in the lab, even when everything else about the institution feels pretty indifferent.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It's hard for me to explain in details without specific questions/prompts, but I feel like over all, I am under the impression that the school and department don't quite care about anything but our performance (e.g. publications, awards, funding, etc.). Social events receive support from the department only when it comes hand-in-hand with speakers or posters, or some sort of academic purposes. There is a lack of support for personal developments, or even interests in non-academic careers, from the department of chemistry at my school.

Coming from a small liberal art college, I don't think I know about many of the research area as I do now. Maybe because many research fields have become "hot topics" in recent years due to the advantage of social media and podcasts (that interesting findings have been better communicated), but an awareness between scientific communities and the general public doesn't hurt. Additionally, I feel like I didn't know at all what to expect from graduate programs. (My undergrad teachers showed me 'the PhD' movie and that was that). Though expectations can be hard because I think working environments are so different even from lab to lab, within a department.

Q26.text: Honestly, pretty broken. It rewards individual achievement over collaboration, and every incentive pushes people toward competition rather than community. I came in thinking research would be this shared, collective endeavor — and instead it feels like everyone's protecting their own territory. it's kind of exhausting.

Q16.text: The loneliness, honestly. I don't think I was prepared for how isolated this would feel. My supervisor is barely around and the other students in the department don't really connect with each other -- we're all just heads down in our own work. it's not what I imagined research would be like.

Q55.text: That the sense of community I was hoping for basically doesn't exist here. I kept thinking I just hadn't found my people yet, but honestly I think its structural -- academia just isn't built for collaboration the way I thought it was. Knowing that earlier would have saved me a lot of disappointment.

Q41.text: Teaching, maybe some outreach work. Research in a light capacity if the environment is more collaborative than this.

Q60.text: Not really. I think I've said most of what I wanted to say -- the isolation, the competitiveness, the way the system just grinds people down. I hope something actually changes but tbh I'm not optimistic.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, I guess. I can follow a question that actually interests me, and that part is genuinely good. And when I do get to talk to undergrads or explain my work to people outside academia, those moments feel meaningful. But honestly those are pockets -- most of the time it's just me alone with my work, which is fine, but its not the rich collaborative thing I came here for.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I can repeat what I wrote above. I think there is too much time alone. I had expected to become part of a creative and established research group, but there is basicaly no group. Everyone is occupied with their own businesses. There is also no proper introduction for phd-students at the department and you are left alone to figure out where to go and what to do. And that you are trained to think egoistic and not collaborative is not constructive! At least not to me.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The unhealthy egoistic culture in academia. I think high-quality research evolves from smart people working together thinking out solutions together, however, the competitiveness between researchers and the little available funding destroy this possibility. I think it is an unhealthy culture to be part of. Furthermore, publications in high-impact journals are valued more than for instance teaching experience and ability when you apply for permanent positions. I think society looses a lot on this, as we end up with a lot of (again) egoistic people at the universities, who then is forced to teach, but feel that it is a waste of time and the result is low-quality teaching.

Q26.text: Honestly, the system is more hierarchical than we expected. There is a lot of dependence on the supervisor relationship -- if it works well, things can flourish, but if there is a power imbalance, it dampens everything. the intellectual environment is stimulating, but that structure makes it hard to develop as truly independent researcher.

Q16.text: The lack of transparency around career pathways has bothered us, honestly. we didn't realize until quite late that a translational research background could open doors at places like Yale or MIT -- had we known that earlier, we might have made very different decisions about where to apply and who to work with.

Q55.text: The power that supervisors hold over every aspect of your trajectory. We knew there would be a supervisor relationship, but didn't fully grasp that it would define -- and sometimes constrain -- almost every decision we made after that. Choosing the right supervisor matters more than choosing the right project, or honestly, even the right institution.

Q60.text: Tbh I think the survey covered most things. If anything, I would say that the conversation around mental health and autonomy in PhD programs needs more urgency -- it's not just individual struggle, its a systemic issue. and we hope research like this actually reaches decision-makers, not just academic journals.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom to pursue questions that actually matter. and honestly, even within frustrating structures, the depth of engagement with a problem -- there's nothing quite like that.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?

Q16.text: What the hell is the point? You do your four years in undergraduate studies and then start graduate studies. Q26.text: O sistema acadêmico da república tcheca é bastante focado em produção.  Não se importa muito a defesa de uma tese, da ideia em si.  Apenas vejo que o programas de PhD em geral esqueceram da onde vem a sigla Ph.D e não discutem mais as coisas no âmbito argumentativo.  Não importam tanto com o racional do projeto, com a hipótese do projeto... e a defesa argumentativa que deveria ser feita.  Maioria dos projetos vejo que começa simplesmente por que temos dinheiro e estrutura. Mas não porque temos um grande racional e uma justificativa para tentar lançar uma hipótese a ser defendida por provas a posteriori.    Na minha concepção,  Tudo deveria iniciar com uma ideia sólida.  Uma hipótese a qual todos não consigam derrubar com argumentos. Sendo interessante alocar recursos escassos para responder uma pergunta da qual necessita-se de uma resposta a posteriori.    O sistema então acaba valorizando bastante dados soltos, contudo ainda sim são resultados. E acaba desvalorizando o tempo 'perdido' no campo das ideias.   A quantidade muitas vezes parece ser mais importante do que a qualidade . Infelizmente vejo que o sistema recompensa este tipo de mentalidade.  No Brasil (país onde fiz meu mestrado), não era diferente.   Com isso , o sistema que criamos é um sistema preocupado com técnicos. Pessoas que vangloriam por saber determinada técnica.  Pois em teoria, isto traz mais produção.  As pessoas não entendem que aprender técnica é apenas uma questão de tempo e prática. Não precisa de raciocínio lógico. Sendo que em muitos institutos grandes, você de fato tem técnicos e facilities para fazer o trabalho técnico para você.   No entanto, técnica pode ser aplicada mil vezes... mas se não estiver denfendendo uma ideia não fará nenhum sentido fazer por fazer.   Acredito que precisamos fazer um esforço para mudar esta mentalidade nos institutos ao redor do mundo.  A revista Nature é muito conceituada e acredito que ela representa bem a amostragem dos institutos que de fato estão preocupados em mover o mundo através de ideias.    Pedro Zeni
